content: Gynaecological cancers are the second most prevalent type of cancer affecting women. It has been proposed that centralising care for these cancers may lead to improved patient outcomes, but there is no clear consensus on this matter. The objective of this study was to evaluate whether centralisation of care for patients with gynaecological cancer is effective in improving outcomes. To conduct this evaluation, a comprehensive search was performed across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Gynaecological Cancer Group Trials Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, and EMBASE, up to November 2010. Additional sources such as clinical trial registries, abstracts from scientific meetings, and reference lists of relevant studies were also reviewed. The inclusion criteria for this analysis encompassed randomised controlled trials (RCTs), quasi-RCTs, controlled before-and-after studies, interrupted time series studies, and observational studies that investigated the centralisation of gynaecological cancer services. Studies were required to use multivariable analysis to adjust for differences in baseline patient characteristics. Three authors independently extracted data from the included studies, and two authors assessed the risk of bias. When possible, survival data were synthesised using meta-analysis techniques. Five studies met the inclusion criteria, but all were retrospective observational studies, which are inherently at high risk of bias. A meta-analysis of three studies involving over 9,000 women with ovarian cancer suggested that treatment at institutions with on-site gynaecologic oncologists was associated with improved survival compared to treatment at community or general hospitals. The hazard ratio (HR) for death was 0.90, with a 95% confidence interval (CI) of 0.82 to 0.99. Similarly, another meta-analysis of three studies involving over 50,000 women with any type of gynaecological cancer found that treatment at teaching hospitals or regional cancer centres was associated with improved survival compared to community or general hospitals. The HR for death in this analysis was 0.91, with a 95% CI of 0.84 to 0.99. The largest of these studies included 48,981 women with various gynaecological malignancies, indicating that the benefits of centralised care extend beyond ovarian cancer. One study compared outcomes between community hospitals with semi-specialised gynaecologists and general hospitals. This study reported a non-significant trend toward better disease-specific survival in women with ovarian cancer treated at community hospitals with semi-specialised gynaecologists (HR 0.89; 95% CI 0.78 to 1.01). Across all included studies, the findings were highly consistent. However, none of the studies reported data on adverse events. The authors concluded that there is low-quality but consistent evidence suggesting that women with gynaecological cancers who receive treatment at specialised centres have longer survival compared to those treated elsewhere. The evidence is particularly stronger for ovarian cancer than for other types of gynaecological cancers. However, further research is needed to confirm these findings, ideally using more robust study designs than retrospective observational studies. Future research should also explore the impact of centralised care on patients' quality of life. Most of the available evidence pertains to ovarian cancer in developed countries, so future studies should also investigate other gynaecological cancers and consider healthcare systems in diverse settings.
